text: , liver, and kidneys.2-5 Combined liver and small intestine transplants are used for patients dependent on parenteral nutrition and with irreversible intestinal and hepatic fail- ure, while intestine-only transplants tend to be used for in- testinal failure in patients with severe progressive compli- cations of parenteral nutrition, such as recurring sepsis and impending loss of central venous access.1,5-8 Multivisceral transplants are most common in patients with diffuse gas- trointestinal motility disorders.3,4 Transplantation of the colon is avoided because of poorer outcomes and in- creased risk of sepsis.9 Overall patient and graft survival varies according to the type of intestinal allograft, and be- tween transplant centres, but is increasing, and reported to be about 50% at 5 years post-transplant.1 Tacrolimus and tapered corticosteroid doses1,2,9-13 are the basis of the standard immunosuppressive regimen. In some centres, corticosteroid-free protocols are used, with induction therapy, and tacrolimus alone as mainte- nance.5,13 Prostaglandins8,9 such as alprostadil may also be given to augment mucosal immunosuppression, and im- prove splanchnic and renal blood flow. Induction therapy with antilymphocyte immunoglobulins or the interleukin- 2 receptor antibodies basiliximab and daclizumab is used to prevent rejection.1,9,11,13-15 Alemtuzumab has also been used.12,13,15 Adjunctive immunosuppressants have been added to the maintenance regimen. Azathioprine has been used.5,11 Sirolimus has also been tried,1,4,8,9,14 but combining tac- rolimus with sirolimus does not have additional benefit over tacrolimus alone.15 Sirolimus maintenance mono- therapy, after induction, is increasingly favoured.15 Any role for mycophenolate mofetil in intestinal transplanta- tion is questionable,12,14,16 owing to its gastrointestinal tox- icity and poor absorption in intestinal transplant recipients, particularly during rejection. Substantial morbidity occurs with intestinal transplants and acute rejection, manifested by diarrhoea, fever, and il- eus, is common.1,2,5,9 Initial treatment is with corticoster- oids, and most centres increase the dose of tacrolimus as well. Antilymphocyte immunoglobulins or muromonab- CD3 may be used for severe or corticosteroid-unrespon- sive episodes.1,2,7,9,13,15 Azathioprine, sirolimus, or myco- phenolate mofetil have also been used adjunctively for treatment of rejection,1,7 although concerns persist about the use of mycophenolate in intestinal transplantation (see above).
